newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait starts diplomatic offensive against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait starts diplomatic offensive against Iraq.

text.p: Kuwait starts a diplomatic offensive on Tuesday to garner support from 1991 Gulf War Arab allies following opposition from some countries to involving themselves in U.S. military strikes against Iraq.
It follows hard on the heels of an intensive round of U.S. lobbying of its Western partners to preserve the old coalition against Iraq's Saddam Hussein.

Opposition by most Arab allies, France and Turkey to direct involvement in possible U.S. military strikes against Iraq is making it difficult for Washington and Kuwait to justify additional action without further splits in the alliance.
Kuwait on Monday agreed to receive more U.S. soldiers and stressed it would not hesitate to take further measures to deter what it sees as threats by former occupier Iraq.
"The (U.S.) ground troops, which are on their way to Kuwait, will be in Kuwait soon, or sooner than later," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said.
"And if there are any other arrangements that need to be taken, in consultation with our allies, we will not hesitate to take them," he told a news conference.

Kuwait's Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah starts a tour on Tuesday of the other five members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to discuss measures taken so far in Washington's current 17-day-old standoff with Iraq.
The oil-rich, Saudi-dominated GCC also groups Oman, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

Sheikh Saud will go on a similar mission to Egypt and Syria, the Arab world's two main military powers which formed the Damascus Declaration alliance with the GCC days after a U.S.-led coalition ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait in 1991.
Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah flew to Britain on Monday night from France following talks in Egypt with President Hosni Mubarak.

Kuwait has strongly defended its decision to allow additional U.S. troops and eight Stealth fighter-bombers to base themselves in Kuwait as part of Washington's military build-up in the Gulf for possible wider strikes against Iraq.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry was in London on Monday to brief French and British counterparts on the Iraq crisis at the end of his Gulf tour. He also visited NATO ally Turkey to secure support for a possible showdown with Iraq.
Britain strongly backed President Bill Clinton's action.

But France has distanced itself from U.S. cruise missile strikes on Iraq earlier this month in retaliation for President Saddam Hussein's sending of troops into northern Kurdish areas to back a faction which has since gained control over the area.
Many U.S. Arab allies and Turkey, Iraq's northern neighbour, gave Perry few concrete signs of support in his search for a tightening of military and economic pressure against Baghdad.
Ankara reiterated that it would not allow U.S. jets to use the Incirlik air base in southern Turkey for bombing raids on Iraq if Washington requested it.
Some key Arab states, including Saudi Arabia, have made similar statements, casting further doubts on the firmness of the international coalition which fought against Iraq.
Kuwait has supported the cruise missile attacks while the small island state of Bahrain said it would allow 23 U.S. F-16s to be based on its territory.
